ideas_declared.rationale: note p.6: MACD line crossing above its own signal line (EMA9 of the MACD line) is the canonical MACD entry trigger. Tested as its own idea, distinct from the zero-line cross -- the note conflates the two, they are not the same signal.

ideas_declared.rationale: note p.6: 'zero line = the momentum midpoint'. MACD crossing zero means EMA12 has just overtaken EMA26 outright -- a coarser, later trigger than the signal-line cross, tested separately at the identical horizon.
ideas_declared.falsifies_if: 10-bar forward hit rate does not exceed the same-bars baseline

ideas_declared.rationale: Matched comparator for the note's own claim (p.6, verbatim): 'MACD crossover is faster but more falsy than MA crossover.' Matched on EMA(10)/EMA(20) rather than SMA(5)/SMA(20) because MACD is itself built from two EMAs (12,26); holding the smoothing family constant isolates the actual mechanical difference this claim is about -- crossing two EMAs directly vs. crossing the EMA12-EMA26 difference against its own EMA9-smoothed signal line -- rather than also changing SMA-vs-EMA responsiveness at the same time.
ideas_declared.falsifies_if: 10-bar forward hit rate does not exceed the same-bars baseline
ideas_declared.source: note p.6 'MACD crossover is faster but more falsy than MA crossover'

ideas_declared.rationale: note p.7: RSI<30 read as the conventional oversold / mean-reversion buy signal. ideas_declared.rationale: note p.2: RSI framed as a 'trend strength regime' indicator rather than a reversion oscillator -- high RSI reads as confirmation of a strong trend worth joining, not exhaustion. Operationalized as a crossing event (entering a strong-momentum regime at 60) rather than a level, at the same horizon and direction as rsi_oversold_reversion so the two opposite readings of the same indicator can be compared head to head.
